ety.text: Ancient Greek γλεῦκος (gleûkos)der. French glucose English glucose From French, from Ancient Greek γλεῦκος (gleûkos, “wine, must”). By surface analysis, gluco- + -ose; note that -ose is derived from the word glucose.

senses.d: A simple monosaccharide (sugar) with a molecular formula of C₆H₁₂O₆; a principle source of energy for cellular metabolism.

ety.text: Coined by French chemist Eugène-Melchior Péligot, from Ancient Greek γλεῦκος (gleûkos, “sweet wine”). By surface analysis, gluco- + -ose.
From gluco- + -osio.
Internationalism. Compare English glucose, glycose. By surface analysis, glico- + -ose.
Internationalism. Borrowed from French glucose. By surface analysis, gluco- + -ose.

Old French glubor. Middle English glew English glue From Middle English glew, glue, from Old French glu (“glue, birdlime”), from Late Latin glūs (stem glūt-), from Latin glūten. Related to clay. Partially displaced native Old English līm (“glue”) and ġelīman (“to glue”) (whence modern lime).

senses.d: A hard gelatin made by boiling bones and hides, used in solution as an adhesive; or any sticky adhesive substance.
Anything that binds two things or people together.
ex: What is a kiss ? Why this, as some approve, / The sure sweet cement, glue, and lime of love.

senses.d: A viscid secretion on the surface of certain plants.
To join or attach something using glue.
ex: I need to glue the chair-leg back into place.

senses.d: To cause something to adhere closely to; to cause to follow attentively.
ex: His eyes were glued to the screen.
Keep your eyes glued to that set until the station signs off. I can assure you that what you will observe is a vast wasteland.

ety.text: Inherited from Vulgar Latin colla, from Ancient Greek κόλλα (kólla, “glue”). Compare Italian colla, Portuguese and Spanish cola.
From Vulgar Latin colla, from Ancient Greek κόλλα (kólla, “glue”). Compare French colle, Sicilian coḍḍa, Spanish and Portuguese cola.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin coda, from Latin cauda, or from its diminutive caudula. Cognate to French queue, Catalan cua, Aragonese coda and Italian coda.
Inherited from Late Latin gumma, from Latin cummi, from Ancient Greek κόμμι (kómmi).
From pegar + -mento.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin colla, from Ancient Greek κόλλα (kólla, “glue”). Compare Spanish cola, French colle, Italian colla.
Inherited from Latin glūten. Doublet of glúten.
colle (“glue”) + -er. First attested in 1320.
From in- + colla + -are.
From en- + cola (“glue”) + -ar.
Inherited from Latin picāre (“smear with pitch”), derived from pix (“pitch”). Compare English pitch.
From cola + -ar. Senses to receive one’s university diploma and to invest are a back-formation from colação.
From Middle French gluten, borrowed from Latin glūten (“glue”).

senses.d: Fibrin (formerly considered as one of the "animal humours").

ex: [H]is nose is running in bubbly gluten over his lips onto his chin […].
The tyrant machine is the female body, grinding and milling the pulp of matter, the gluten of human flesh.

senses.d: The major protein in cereal grains, especially wheat; responsible for the elasticity in dough and the structure in baked bread.
A gluey, sticky mass of clay, bitumen etc.
ex: Despite constant rain that turned roads to gluten, the Yankees kept moving.
